title: Wilt thou be made whole (John 5:1–9)
hook: a man ill thirty-eight years is asked if he wants to be healed
tomorrow: I am the bread of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, fields white for harvest, and the Samaritans coming up the road. Your line was lift up your eyes. Who did you notice when you looked up? Day five hundred two.

In Jerusalem, near the sheep gate, there's a pool with five porches, covered walkways around the water. The Douay-Rheims calls it Probatica, from the Greek for sheep; most Bibles know it as Bethesda. The porches are full of people: the blind, the lame, the withered, lying on mats, waiting. People said that now and then the water was stirred, and the first one in would be healed. One man has been lying there a very long time. Thirty-eight years, John tells us, under his illness. Today Jesus walks into that crowd, finds him, and asks him a question that sounds almost rude.
screen: `A POOL WITH FIVE PORCHES.` → `A CROWD WAITING FOR THE WATER.` → `THIRTY-EIGHT YEARS.`

segments.voice: Jesus sees him lying there, knows he has been that way a long time, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Do you want to get well? On the surface, it's an absurd question. Of course he does. He has been lying by a healing pool for thirty-eight years. But listen to his answer. He doesn't say yes. "Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pond." Someone always gets there first. It's an explanation, and a lonely one: nobody to help, every time. After thirty-eight years, the story he tells about his life has become: it's never going to be me. Jesus doesn't argue with the story. He doesn't carry him to the water. He says: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk." And immediately the man is made whole, picks up his mat, and walks. The question matters because healing would change everything. A man who has been ill for thirty-eight years has a whole life built around it: a place to lie, a way of asking, a way of being seen. Being made whole means standing up into a life he doesn't know yet. The Church teaches that God respects our freedom, even in healing; grace is offered, not forced. Two honest notes. Some old manuscripts include a verse about an angel stirring the water; many of the earliest leave it out, and modern Catholic Bibles often put it in a footnote. And this pool is real. Archaeologists near the Church of Saint Anne in Jerusalem found two large pools with a wall between them, which some think explains the five porches.
screen: `WILT THOU BE MADE WHOLE?` · `SIR, I HAVE NO MAN.` · `ARISE, TAKE UP THY BED.` · `A REAL POOL BY SAINT ANNE'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer that question honestly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you've been stuck a long time. A habit, a hurt, a fear, a resentment, a relationship gone flat. Then hear the question, gently: do you want to be made whole? Notice your first answer. Is it a yes, or is it a reason, like his: nobody helps, someone always gets there first? Don't judge it. Just hear it. If you pray, you can give God your honest answer. If you don't, just let yourself know what it is. The bell holds the time.
Wilt thou be made whole. Jesus's question to a man ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda, before he told him to rise and walk. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: wilt thou be made whole. Today, take one small step toward the thing you said you wanted, before the reasons start. Day five hundred two.

original.note: Greek: whole, healthy, sound (John 5:6). The root of the English word hygiene.

trapdoor: what you thought: an obvious question to a sick man.
what it means: being made whole means standing up into a new life, and Jesus asks before he heals.
what a scholar hears: the verse about the angel stirring the water (5:3b–4) is missing from many early manuscripts; excavations at Saint Anne's show two pools.

notes: Douay John 5:2 names the pool 'Probatica' and says it is called in Hebrew 'Bethsaida'; most modern Bibles read Bethesda. The script says 'most Bibles know it as Bethesda'. Confirm.
John 5:3b–4 (the angel) is absent from many early manuscripts and footnoted in the NABRE; stated generally. Confirm.
Excavations at St Anne's (two pools with a central dividing wall, possibly the fifth portico): confirm phrasing.
'The Church teaches that God respects our freedom' (softened in review from 'has always taught') — general (cf. CCC 1730–1742); confirm.
Original: ὑγιής and its link to 'hygiene' (via Hygieia): confirm.
